source: FAO/OIE/World Bank, "Good Practices for Biosecurity in the Pig Sector - Issues and Options in Developing and Transition Countries", FAO Animal Production and Health Paper No. 169, Rome, 2010.
text: Pig diseases can be grouped by how they behave and their impact: transboundary/epidemic diseases (foot-and-mouth disease, African swine fever, classical swine fever/hog cholera, and pseudorabies) are highly contagious viral diseases with potential for high mortality and severe economic impact, and are the top biosecurity priority; other severe infectious diseases like porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS) and swine influenza can occur in waves and sometimes persist in a herd over long periods; endemic production diseases are present in many pig populations worldwide but their severity depends heavily on herd management, hygiene and husbandry quality - good practices can keep the same pathogen from causing serious clinical disease; and zoonotic diseases (such as Streptococcus suis, leptospirosis, and Japanese encephalitis) can pass from pigs to the people who handle them, which is a reason to avoid handling sick pigs bare-handed and to cook pork thoroughly.
